https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.title: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/ai-startu.author: Camila Grigera Naón
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars.

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune.

Blue Cloud Ventures led the round, bringing Numa’s total funding to $96 million. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participated. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson. The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare, accounting and consulting firm KPMG found that 34% reported widespread employee adoption of AI agents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 25% in the first quarter.
For Roumeliotis, Numa began with a familiar team and a new problem to solve.

He had previously built Location Labs, a mobile technology company that tapped into the early spread of GPS-enabled cellphones to help people track one another’s locations. After selling the business in 2015, he joined venture firm Draper Fisher Jurvetson as an entrepreneur-in-residence.

While he was there, former colleagues from Location Labs approached him with a proposition: They wanted to build another company together. The group included engineers, product specialists and executives who had taken on bigger roles under Roumeliotis.

In 2017, they launched Number AI to help small businesses receive and respond to texts through their existing landline numbers, using natural language processing to bring newer technology to businesses still relying on older tools.

But as they worked with car dealerships, they found problems that went beyond missed messages. Employees juggled calls, paperwork and manual follow-ups, leaving customers waiting. The team narrowed its focus to the automotive industry and renamed the company Numa.
Blue Cloud Ventures also saw an opportunity in dealerships still relying on older software.

“I look at the auto dealership… as a little bit like jumbo shrimp. It’s a massive niche,” Mir Arif, the venture capital firm’s managing partner, told Fortune. “All of them [are still] working off legacy software or literally pen and paper.”

Today, the company has about 160 employees across its Bay Area headquarters, a sales and marketing office in Kansas City and an AI development office in Montreal. More than 1,500 dealerships in the U.S. and Canada use its software, including Longo Toyota, Norm Reeves Honda and Gold Coast Cadillac.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/arist-ceo.title: AI could soon be telling CEOs whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision making is so much faster’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/16/arist-ceo.author: Tatiana Sataua
paragraphs: AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, said while speaking with Fortune‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely.
“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe said.

That prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported, HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with consultants to understand why. He believes AI can help executives get answers in days rather than months.

Ioffe didn’t set out to compete with consulting firms. At 19, he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform, then shifted Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies, becoming one of OpenAI’s early partners along the way.

He started to notice a pattern: companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem, then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it. In his experience, the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time.

That prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing the problems companies were trying to solve. Ioffe pointed to a major software company whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why.

Before AI can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it first needs to understand what’s happening inside a company. Arist’s agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions, and weigh responses against information such as an employee’s tenure, performance, and past engagement scores. Ioffe said that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization. The agents will also push back, he said, if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want.

But gathering that information could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an AI agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.
Ioffe argued that employees may actually be more candid with AI agents than with another person, making it easier for companies to uncover problems that might otherwise go unreported.
“Turns out that humans are not that good at listening,” he quipped.
Rather than replacing executives or consultants, Ioffe sees AI’s biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster.
“If you can get to the truth much faster, then a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup,” Ioffe said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/17/pantera-b.title: Pantera-backed Codex raises $30 million to link Asia to global markets with stablecoins
https://fortune.com/2026/11/17/pantera-b.author: Camila Grigera Naón
paragraphs: Money might make the world go round—but that doesn’t mean getting it around the world is easy. And while stablecoins, or cryptocurrencies pegged to fiat money, can simplify the process considerably, many businesses still lack the infrastructure to use them for cross-border payments. That’s where Codex sees an opportunity.

The Delaware-based startup announced Tuesday it raised $30 million in a Series A round to help businesses send money across borders and exchange currencies, without the need to deposit money in advance to use the service. Codex aims to carve out a niche in Asia and connect the region to markets in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa.

“We help people convert money into whatever form they want and give it to whoever they want, wherever they want,” Haonan Li, cofounder and CEO of Codex, told Fortune. “Turns out, in lots of parts of the world, this is actually super hard to do.”

The 35-person company plans to use part of the capital to further automate its foreign-exchange platform, with AI agents central to its vision for how the business will operate, and keep costs down as transaction volumes grow.

Pantera Capital led the round, with participation from Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures, at a $130 million post-money valuation. Both participated in Codex’s earlier seed round, which Dragonfly led alongside backers Circle Ventures, Cumberland, and Wintermute.

Stablecoins have been one of cryptocurrency’s longest-lasting trends, gaining traction as a lifeline in countries with high inflation or capital controls, and as a low-cost payment tool for businesses. Payments made with stablecoins reached at least $401 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 42% year over year, with businesses on the receiving end of an estimated 58% to 64% of that volume, according to a September report by global consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal.

“[The team] is building Codex to meet the challenge of what happens after this massive explosion of stablecoin issuance, which is… a really fragmented system,” Franklin Bi general partner at Pantera Capital, said.

An economist by training, Li began his career in geopolitical forecasting research for political psychologist and writer Philip Tetlock, followed by a stint in quantitative finance. He later caught the “crypto bug” and became an early employee at Optimism, where he worked on Ethereum scaling and protocol economics.

There, he began to explore crypto’s most practical applications and landed on stablecoins, which some in Ethereum circles dismissed as boring. Li saw a way to help people excluded from traditional financial networks save, transfer, and exchange money.

To build that business, he teamed up with an old friend from his military days. Li had met Victor Yaw, now a Codex cofounder, about a decade earlier in infantry officer candidate school in Singapore’s military. Fellow cofounder Momo Ong, whom Li met through San Francisco’s founder community, initially advised the team before he joined full time. Together, they founded Codex in 2024.

After a few iterations, the company settled on its current product about a year ago. It now has offices in Singapore, Hong Kong and London, as well as New York and San Francisco. As Li put it: “the journey stretched from the jungles of Brunei to the skyscrapers of New York.”

金钱或许可以让世界运转起来，但这并不意味着让金钱运转起来很容易。尽管稳定币或与法定货币挂钩的加密货币可以大大简化流程，但许多企业仍然缺乏使用它们进行跨境支付的基础设施。这就是 Codex 看到的机会。

这家总部位于特拉华州的初创公司周二宣布，在 A 轮融资中筹集了 3000 万美元，帮助企业跨境汇款和兑换货币，而无需提前存钱即可使用该服务。 Codex 旨在在亚洲开拓市场，并将该地区与拉丁美洲和撒哈拉以南非洲市场连接起来。

Codex 联合创始人兼首席执行官李浩南向《财富》杂志表示：“我们帮助人们将金钱转换成他们想要的任何形式，并随时随地将其送给任何他们想要的人。” “事实证明，在世界许多地方，这实际上是非常难做到的。”

这家拥有 35 名员工的公司计划利用部分资金进一步自动化其外汇平台，人工智能代理将成为其业务运营愿景的核心，并随着交易量的增长降低成本。

Pantera Capital 领投，Dragonfly 和 Coinbase Ventures 跟投，投后估值为 1.3 亿美元。两人都参与了 Codex 的早期种子轮融资，由 Dragonfly 与支持者 Circle Ventures、Cumberland 和 Wintermute 共同领投。

稳定币一直是加密货币最持久的趋势之一，作为高通胀或资本管制国家的生命线以及企业的低成本支付工具而受到关注。根据全球咨询公司 Alvarez & Marsal 9 月份的一份报告，2026 年前 8 个月，使用稳定币支付的金额至少达到 4010 亿美元，同比增长 42%，其中企业接收的金额预计占 58% 至 64%。

Pantera Capital 普通合伙人 Franklin Bi 表示：“[团队]正在构建 Codex，以应对稳定币发行大规模爆炸后所发生的挑战，这是一个非常分散的系统。”

作为一名训练有素的经济学家，李开始了他的职业生涯，为政治心理学家和作家菲利普·泰洛克进行地缘政治预测研究，随后在量化金融领域工作了一段时间。后来他发现了“加密货币错误”，并成为 Optimism 的早期员工，在那里他从事以太坊扩展和协议经济学工作。

在那里，他开始探索加密货币最实际的应用，并最终选择了稳定币，但以太坊圈子里的一些人认为稳定币很无聊。李找到了一种方法来帮助那些被排除在传统金融网络之外的人们储蓄、转移和兑换货币。

为了开展这项业务，他与一位军旅时期的老朋友合作。大约十年前，李在新加坡军队的步兵军官候补学校认识了 Victor Yaw，他现在是 Codex 的联合创始人。李通过旧金山的创始人社区结识了联合创始人之一的 Momo Ong，他在全职加入之前最初为团队提供了建议。他们于 2024 年共同创立了 Codex。

经过几次迭代后，该公司大约一年前确定了当前的产品。目前，该公司在新加坡、香港、伦敦以及纽约和旧金山设有办事处。正如李所说：“旅程从文莱的丛林延伸到纽约的摩天大楼。”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/25/exclusive.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
https://fortune.com/2026/11/25/exclusive.author: Sebastian Herrera
paragraphs: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how exactly Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer.

Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, the people said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they said.

Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year. This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.

AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries. Agentic shopping could total $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, representing 10% to 20% of the total market, according to a 2025 report by Morgan Stanley. Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.

Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements. Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and have autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars and booking reservations. As of October, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up the app, making it Meta’s biggest consumer AI hit to date. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.

“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month in a call with analysts. “We’d like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business. Advertising has become a $68.6 billion business for Amazon, representing nearly 10% of its total yearly revenue. In October, Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Still, Jassy said this month at a Semafor conference that Amazon hadn’t ruled out letting outside shopping agents into its store, but that they would have to provide a “fair exchange of value.”

Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent. Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.

Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before. In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps. Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases. The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.

Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy. Retailers have gained another channel for selling products, while Meta tries to grow Muse and, according to Zuckerberg, eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”

“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month in a call with analysts. “We’d like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business. Advertising has become a $68.6 billion business for Amazon, representing nearly 10% of its total yearly revenue. In October, Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”

Still, Jassy said this month at a Semafor conference that Amazon hadn’t ruled out letting outside shopping agents into its store, but that they would have to provide a “fair exchange of value.”

Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent. Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.

Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before. In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps. Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases. The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.

Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy. Retailers have gained another channel for selling products, while Meta tries to grow Muse and, according to Zuckerberg, eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
